title: There's No 25th Amendment for Congress
hook: When a president is incapacitated, the Constitution has a formal fix: the 25th Amendment. When a senator is hospitalized for weeks with no details given, there isn't one.
key_points: The 25th Amendment lets the vice president and Cabinet formally declare a president unable to serve, temporarily transferring power.
No equivalent constitutional mechanism exists for Congress — a senator or representative can remain in office through a long illness with no formal disclosure required.
A chamber can expel its own member, but only by a two-thirds vote, and that power has historically been used for misconduct, not health.
In 2026, Sen. Mitch McConnell's weeks-long hospitalization renewed calls for more transparency about lawmakers' health, following earlier cases of prolonged, undisclosed absences.
Absent a constitutional requirement, whatever disclosure happens depends on the choices of the lawmaker, their office, and their party.
content_html: The Constitution anticipated that a president might become unable to do the job, and built a formal process for it: the 25th Amendment lets the vice president and Cabinet declare the president incapacitated and temporarily hand off power. Congress never got an equivalent.
extra_html: That gap became visible again in 2026, when Sen. Mitch McConnell was hospitalized for nearly four weeks with scant public detail, NPR's Sam Gringlas reported — not the first time in recent memory a member of Congress has been absent for an extended stretch without much explanation. A chamber can expel one of its own members, but only with a two-thirds vote, a threshold and a tool historically reserved for misconduct rather than illness. Short of that, nothing in the Constitution requires a senator or representative to disclose a health condition or step aside — whatever transparency exists is a matter of individual, office, or party choice, not law. (This card describes the U.S. Congress specifically.)

related.title: The Legislature
related.hook: The branch that makes the law is also where a society argues out loud — the legislature turns competing interests into binding rules through debate and votes.

related.title: Checks and Balances
related.hook: Separating power isn't enough — each branch also gets tools to limit the others, so power keeps power in check.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

flashcards.prompt: What does the 25th Amendment do, and why doesn't it help with an incapacitated member of Congress?
flashcards.back_html: It lets the vice president and Cabinet formally declare a president unable to serve. It applies only to the presidency — Congress has no constitutional equivalent for its own members.

flashcards.prompt: How can a chamber of Congress remove one of its own incapacitated or absent members?

choices.text: Only by a two-thirds expulsion vote, a power historically used for misconduct rather than health
A simple majority vote of the full chamber, for any reason
The president can remove them directly

flashcards.explanation_html: Expulsion is the formal mechanism, but its high threshold and historical use make it a poor fit for handling illness or incapacity.

flashcards.prompt: What determines how much a lawmaker discloses about a serious health issue?

choices.text: Their own choice, and that of their office and party — there's no constitutional disclosure requirement
A binding federal transparency law requiring full medical disclosure
Automatic disclosure triggered after a fixed number of missed votes

flashcards.explanation_html: Unlike the presidency's 25th Amendment process, Congress has no formal rule forcing disclosure — it depends entirely on individual choices.
